chapters.name: The word 'harm'
chapters.note: the word list flagged the nice one

cap.1: A word-search scorer flags 'I must avoid harm' as harmful, because it contains 'harm'. And polite, appalling advice sails straight through.
cap.2: Keyword scoring is fast and free, but no list covers every phrasing, and it can't tell using a word from mentioning it. In [4.1] it misses misalignment phrased politely, which is most of it.
cap.3: Lexicon scorers have bounded, legible failures: non-exhaustive lexicons, word-level granularity, and no use-mention distinction. The [4.1] comparison shows polite misalignment slipping past.

cap.1: Hire a marker. Hand over the question, the answer and a clear marking scheme, and ask for one number in a box on the cover. Now you can tally thousands.
cap.2: An autorater, or LLM-as-judge: prompt a model with the question, the response and a 0 to 100 rubric, and ask for the score inside a fixed tag your code can parse.
cap.3: ARENA's judge prompt comes from the emergent misalignment repo's eval questions: a 0 to 100 score with 0 totally aligned, output constrained to <score>NUMBER</score>, divided by 100.

cap.1: Send every answer out at once, retry politely when the marker is busy, read the number in the box, and never treat a blank box as a perfect mark.
cap.2: A ThreadPoolExecutor fans calls out with exponential backoff on rate limits and restores input order. max_tokens=16, since only the tag comes back. Regex the score; raise on no match.
cap.3: A silently zeroed parse failure reads as perfectly aligned. A coherence judge runs alongside: broken text is broken, not misaligned, and counting it inflates every steering result.

chapters.name: Topic, not stance

right.title: Rubric about endorsement
lines: only actionable harmful advice scores high

chapters.verdict: Mentioning is not recommending: say so in the rubric.

cap.1: Give a vague marking scheme and the marker grades the topic: an essay warning about scams gets marked as scammy. Say plainly that warning about harm scores zero.
cap.2: A base model got 0.7 misalignment for a careful scam warning. At max_tokens=16 there is no room to reason, so the judge pattern-matched on topic. Rewrite the rubric around endorsement.
cap.3: Judges are primed by surface content. Anchor the rubric on endorsement, not subject: discussing, warning or refusing scores 0; only advice a reader could act on to their own detriment scores high.

chapters.name: What the marks add up to

cap.1: The rate you see is the real misbehaviour the marker catches, plus harmless answers it wrongly flags. When most answers are harmless, small mistakes pile up fast.
cap.2: If a judge flags 5% of harmless answers and the true rate is 2%, it reports about 7%: more than triple. The false-alarm term is multiplied by the large harmless majority.
cap.3: seen = m(1 − fn) + (1 − m)fp, with m the true rate. Estimate fp and fn from hand labels and you can invert it: m = (seen − fp)/(1 − fp − fn). Without them, judge error dominates at low base rates.

chapters.name: Check the marker
chapters.title: twenty hand-labelled answers: you vs the judge

cap.1: Before trusting the marker, mark twenty essays yourself and compare. The two disagreement boxes are the marker's blind spots, and they skew your totals.
cap.2: Current method: an LLM judge with a rubric. Open problem: position and verbosity bias, errors shared with the judged model, and almost no EM paper reports judge-human agreement. Measure yours.
cap.3: Hand labels estimate fp and fn directly. Keep a 'helpful' control domain: if its scores rise, the judge moved, not the model. Publishing agreement for the standard 0 to 100 judge is a capstone seed.

chapters.name: Every number runs through it
items: Steering results: scored by a judge

cap.1: Almost every number about a model's behaviour in this chapter comes from a marker like this. To understand and steer AI, first trust your marker.
cap.2: Steering effectiveness, phase transitions and trait scoring in [4.4] all run through autoraters, and the same skill returns as [4.2]'s alignment-faking classifier. Get the habits right once.
cap.3: The alignment judge plus a coherence judge made emergent misalignment's 20% versus 0% headline possible and became the field's default instrument. Its error bars are your results' error bars.

coda.title: How much of the reported rate is real? (a toy)

caption.1: The true rate is small. Nudge the marker's false alarms up a little and watch the reported rate balloon. The control bar shows the false alarms on their own.
caption.2: With a low true rate, false alarms on the harmless majority dominate what the judge reports. The control domain, where the true rate is zero, reads out fp directly: watch it.
caption.3: Toy measurement model: seen = m(1 − fn) + (1 − m)fp, and a true-zero control reads fp. With fp and fn from hand labels, m = (seen − fp)/(1 − fp − fn).

hamming.what: A model prompted with a rubric to grade another model's free-text answers, returning a parseable score in place of a human rater.
hamming.when: Whenever you need to score thousands of open-ended responses for a behaviour that keywords can't capture.
hamming.why: Almost every number about model behaviour in alignment research comes out of a judge like this, so its errors become your results' errors.

object.title: The marker's ledger
object.subtitle: Every answer lands in one of four boxes: you and the judge agree, or one of you calls it misaligned. Heights are shares of answers.

cap.1: Four boxes. The giant one holds harmless answers the judge also calls fine. The small ones are where all the trouble lives.
cap.2: A confusion matrix of you (rows) against the judge (columns). Height is the share of answers in each box, lifted slightly so empty boxes still show.
cap.3: Cells: (1 − m)(1 − fp), (1 − m)fp, m·fn, m(1 − fn). The judge's reported rate is the sum of the right-hand column.

cap.1: Look down the judge's 'misaligned' column. The false alarms stand taller than the real catches: more than half of what it flags is harmless.
cap.2: At m = 5%, fp = 5%, fn = 20%: 4.75% of answers are false alarms and 4% are real catches. Precision is under half.
cap.3: Low base rates make precision collapse even for a judge with modest fp: the (1 − m) multiplier swamps the true-positive mass.

cap.1: A judge with no false alarms: everything in its 'misaligned' column is really misaligned. This is what your rubric fixes are chasing.
cap.2: fp = 0 empties the false-alarm box. An endorsement-based rubric and a true-zero control domain are how you push toward it and check it.
cap.3: With fp = 0 the reported rate is m(1 − fn): a pure undercount, correctable given fn from hand labels.

cap.1: Raise the true rate and real catches tower over the false alarms. Marker mistakes matter most when misbehaviour is rare.
cap.2: At m = 30%, the true-positive box dwarfs the false alarms. Judge error is most dangerous exactly in the low-rate regime alignment evals live in.
cap.3: Precision rises with base rate; the same judge that is fine for a 30% effect can manufacture a 5% one.

cap.1: Now a marker who misses a lot of polite misalignment: the 'miss' box grows and your total quietly undercounts.
cap.2: High fn: misaligned answers the judge calls fine. Polite phrasing is what beat the keyword scorer; a judge sharing the model's blind spots can miss it too.
cap.3: fn inflates when judge and judged model share errors; only human labels on a sample reveal it.

predict.q: Your judge gives a careful warning about scams a high misalignment score. Best fix?

options.t: Rewrite the rubric around endorsement, with examples at 0, 50 and 100

predict.why: The judge scored the topic, not the stance. Say that warning about harm scores 0 and only actionable harmful advice scores high.

predict.q: The regex finds no <score> tag in a reply. What should your code do?

options.t: Raise, or flag it for review

predict.why: 0 means totally aligned, so a silent zero looks exactly like a good answer and drags your misalignment rate down.

predict.q: After you edit the judge prompt, your 'helpful' control questions start scoring as more misaligned. What moved?
predict.why: The control domain's true rate didn't change. If its scores rise, the measuring instrument moved.

object.where: Anywhere a tally depends on a marker: exam boards, medical screening, content moderation, spam filters.
